articles.title: Origins and historical context
articles.summary: Separate the original game, regional publishing and community projects.
articles.scope: Historical North American producer account from May 2008. This is not a worldwide release chronology.

blocks.heading: Developer and regional launch
blocks.body: Producer Joshua Sell identified the Korean company SonoV as Shaiya's developer and described a December 2007 commercial opening in his North American interview. This date is not presented here as the original Korean launch.

blocks.heading: What still needs verification
blocks.body: An exact Korean launch chronology and later regional publishing changes require additional primary sources. They are intentionally not filled in from unsourced timelines.

articles.title: Factions, roles and progression
articles.summary: A compact introduction to the historical game structure.
articles.scope: Historical description from 2008; class balance, level caps and progression rules can differ on later or customized servers.

blocks.heading: The two factions
blocks.body: Alliance of Light includes Humans and Elves; Union of Fury includes Vail and Nordein. Historical class pairs cover melee damage, tanking, ranged damage, stealth, healing and magic.

blocks.heading: PvE and PvP
blocks.body: Quests, monsters, experience and equipment support progression; faction conflict and battlegrounds support PvP. The producer also described faction blessings.

blocks.heading: Difficulty modes
blocks.body: The historical interview discusses Easy, Normal, Hard and Ultimate modes, including a character-loss risk in Ultimate. Check your service's current rules rather than assuming those historical conditions still apply.

articles.title: Programming languages and episode labels
articles.summary: Distinguish documented community code from the original proprietary game.
articles.scope: The complete original technology stack is not established by the sources reviewed for this edition.

blocks.heading: What can be stated
blocks.body: Imgeneus describes itself as a C#/.NET server project. Parsec is a .NET library for Shaiya formats. Those statements describe these community projects, not the language of every original client and server component.

blocks.heading: Episode is not a complete compatibility specification
blocks.body: Record the episode label, region, file version and exact package alongside a project. The archive separates regional builds. An episode name alone does not establish matching binaries, data layouts or configuration.

articles.title: ps_Game and companion services
articles.summary: Read the service layout before changing a server installation.
articles.scope: Static inspection of the EP6.4 Essentials archive identified in the sources. Service internals and startup behavior were not executed or reverse-engineered.

blocks.heading: The game-service configuration
blocks.body: The inspected PSM_Client/Bin/Config/ps_game.ini has SERVER, CONNECTION, DB and GAMEINFO sections. It references Session, DBAgent, UserLog and GameLog connections, plus GameDef and GameData database settings. This shows the game service is part of a multi-component installation, not a standalone executable with all data embedded.

blocks.heading: Companion configuration files
blocks.body: ps_login.ini contains a UserData database setting and Session/UserLog connections. ps_dbAgent.ini contains a GameData setting. ps_session.ini contains a GAMESERVERS section. These are confirmed configuration references; exact authentication, persistence and session logic still depends on the binaries.

blocks.heading: A useful starting checklist
blocks.body: Identify the actual running executable and the configuration path it reads. Keep the package inventory with your project. A familiar service name does not prove that an executable copied from another episode is compatible.

articles.title: Configuration files and endpoints
articles.summary: Understand which values need local review without copying somebody else's credentials.
articles.scope: EP6.4 Essentials configuration keys only. No credentials, addresses or fixed port prescriptions are reproduced.

blocks.heading: Keys to locate
blocks.body: The inspected ps_game.ini contains ServerPort, GamePublicIP and GameVersion. It also contains database and companion-service connection settings. Review each in the context of your own package; a listening port and a publicly advertised address serve different configuration purposes.

blocks.heading: Working copies versus deployment templates
blocks.body: This archive contains configuration under both PSM_Client/Bin/Config and PSM_Server/ShaiyaServerPatch/Config. Finding two files with the same name does not establish which one a running process uses. Confirm the working directory and deployment mechanism before editing.

blocks.heading: Recommended editing workflow
blocks.body: Back up the exact file, record the previous value locally, change one setting, and inspect the relevant log after a controlled restart. Keep passwords out of screenshots and shared issue reports. This is guidance, not a tested installation recipe.

articles.title: GameVersion, build and protocol
articles.summary: A version field is not a universal episode conversion switch.
articles.scope: EP6.4 configuration inspection plus community protocol documentation. No universal GameVersion number is asserted.

blocks.heading: Two different observations
blocks.body: GameVersion is present in the inspected game-service configuration. OpenShaiya documents a client version field in ServerSelectRequest. These observations do not prove that every release uses the same number, comparison rule or packet layout.

blocks.heading: When investigating a mismatch
blocks.body: Record the complete client build and server package. Compare the package documentation and logs before changing values. Making a version check pass would not, by itself, convert item structures, packet layouts or map data between episodes.

articles.title: SQL Server, databases and SSMS
articles.summary: Separate the storage engine, the data and the management application.
articles.scope: SQL Server concepts; Shaiya examples refer only to the inspected legacy scripts and package.

blocks.heading: The three layers
blocks.body: SQL Server is the database service. Its databases contain structured objects such as tables and stored procedures; table rows hold records. SSMS is a management application used to connect to the service and inspect or administer it. Installing SSMS alone does not install a Shaiya database.

blocks.heading: Names found in this collection
blocks.body: The inspected scripts reference PS_UserData.dbo.Users_Master, PS_GameData.dbo.Chars, PS_GameData.dbo.CharItems and PS_GameDefs.dbo.Items. These are examples from this collection, not a promise that every server uses the same schema.

blocks.heading: Why the distinction matters
blocks.body: A connection can succeed while the expected database or object is absent. Confirm the SQL instance, database and object names separately before treating a problem as a game-client failure.

articles.title: Characters, item definitions and item records
articles.summary: Read the actual schema before writing a query.
articles.scope: Object references verified in the linked legacy scripts; keys, constraints and synchronization behavior require inspection of your database.

blocks.heading: Definition and ownership are different questions
blocks.body: The collection references both PS_GameDefs.dbo.Items and PS_GameData.dbo.CharItems, alongside Chars. Treat an item definition and a character-owned item record as different concepts. Do not assume that a display name, item type and unique owned-item identifier can be used interchangeably.

blocks.heading: Inspect before joining or updating
blocks.body: Read column types, indexes and any relevant procedures in your own test database. The scripts in the collection are historical examples, not validated migrations. Editing a row does not establish when a running game service will reload or overwrite it.

blocks.heading: Read-only discovery example
blocks.body: In SSMS, first select the intended test database. This query lists the user tables visible to your account. It changes no data and is shown for reading/copying only; shDeveloperTools does not connect to SQL or execute it. An incomplete list can reflect permissions.

articles.title: Backups and safe changes
articles.summary: A useful backup is one you can restore.
articles.scope: General SQL Server guidance; no backup or restore was performed against a Shaiya server.

blocks.heading: Plan the restore as well as the backup
blocks.body: Use SQL Server's backup facilities and keep copies separate from the working database. Practice restoring to a separate test environment, then check that the expected data is available. A file existing on disk does not demonstrate a successful recovery.

blocks.heading: Before changing game data
blocks.body: Record which database and server a change targets. Test the query against a restored copy, review its selection criteria, and plan how to recover. Coordinate changes with the game services so that active writes do not undermine the intended result.

blocks.heading: What this app does today
blocks.body: This library explains the workflow. It does not currently schedule SQL backups, run queries or restore databases. Those would be separate features with explicit connection and operation controls.

articles.title: data.sah, data.saf and client resources
articles.summary: Start with the archive pair and an episode-aware reader.
articles.scope: Community format documentation and observed OpenShaiya client inventories; not an official specification for every episode.

blocks.heading: The archive pair
blocks.body: Shaiya tooling treats data.sah and data.saf together when loading resource archives. Parsec documents extraction, rebuilding and patching of this pair. Preserve matching copies instead of replacing one file from an unrelated client.

blocks.heading: Reader compatibility
blocks.body: Parsec documents format testing for Episodes 5, 6 and 8 and cautions that other episodes may differ. A parser successfully opening a file is a starting point, not proof that every field can be edited correctly.

articles.title: SData and episode-dependent layouts
articles.summary: Recognize resource names without assuming universal binary structures.
articles.scope: The linked Parsec documentation describes its own supported formats and tested episodes.

blocks.heading: Examples of supported formats
blocks.body: Parsec lists Item.SData, Skill.SData, Monster.SData, NpcQuest.SData and several world/model formats. It also distinguishes older SData handling from Episode 8 variants.

blocks.heading: Choose explicit assumptions
blocks.body: Select the intended episode and text encoding when the tool supports those choices. Export a small sample and check the resulting fields before planning a bulk transformation. Keep this work on a copy.

articles.title: Matching a client to a server
articles.summary: Keep build identity with your development files.
articles.scope: Recommended workflow based on regional archive organization and community protocol documentation.

blocks.heading: Record a reproducible baseline
blocks.body: Keep the original download URL, archive size and a local SHA-256 alongside the region, episode label and intended server package. Record any patches separately. This makes later comparisons more useful than a folder named latest.

blocks.heading: Do not confuse different versions
blocks.body: An updater's patch number, an executable's file version and a protocol version are not automatically the same identifier. OpenShaiya documents a protocol version field; the archive also uses regional and build labels. Confirm which identifier a particular configuration actually expects.

articles.title: What shStudio is for
articles.summary: A purpose-built editor with version-specific capabilities.
articles.scope: Summary of the tool author's release/manual thread. It is not a compatibility test of every shStudio download in this library.

blocks.heading: Documented responsibilities
blocks.body: The author describes shStudio as a multi-purpose editor for client and server configuration resources. The manual covers workspaces, archives, server files, SQL connections and editors for resources including items and skills.

blocks.heading: Choose a matching release
blocks.body: Check the manual and release notes for the actual editor build you use. Do not assume that the newest editor supports every old or customized file. Start with a workspace copy and inspect exported output before applying changes to a server.

articles.title: A repeatable editing workflow
articles.summary: Make a small change you can compare and undo.
articles.scope: Workflow recommendation; each file format and editor still needs its own compatibility check.

blocks.heading: Keep an original and a working copy
blocks.body: Record the archive and editor versions. Make one small edit in a copy, save to a new output, and compare the changed files. Avoid mixing a bulk format conversion with balance changes in the same experiment.

blocks.heading: Validate in a test environment
blocks.body: Reopen the output in a compatible reader, then test its intended behavior with the matching client and server. A successful export does not prove that gameplay, text encoding or linked resources are correct. Keep a short change log so the result can be reproduced.

articles.title: Visual Studio and source projects
articles.summary: Use an IDE for projects whose source code you actually have.
articles.scope: Official Visual Studio capabilities; suggested Shaiya-related uses are development ideas, not included app features.

blocks.heading: What the IDE provides
blocks.body: Visual Studio combines source editing, building, debugging and testing. It is appropriate for your own desktop utilities, services and compatible source projects. Imgeneus is one example of a community Shaiya server implemented in C#/.NET.

blocks.heading: A useful boundary
blocks.body: Downloading a compiled game executable does not supply the original editable source project. Plan new utilities around documented formats and source you can inspect; installing an IDE alone does not make an arbitrary executable rebuildable.

articles.title: VS Code for configuration and documentation
articles.summary: Keep small text changes easy to review.
articles.scope: Official VS Code overview; suggested workflow for your local project copies.

blocks.heading: Useful everyday tasks
blocks.body: VS Code is a code editor suitable for text-oriented work such as JSON catalogs, configuration copies, scripts and documentation. Its project navigation and editing tools help keep related files together.

blocks.heading: Use the right tool for the data
blocks.body: A text editor is not a Shaiya binary-format editor. Use a compatible parser for binary resources. For configuration and catalog work, keep changes small and validate the result before distributing it. Extensions and runtimes are separate dependencies, not automatically provided by opening a file.

articles.title: XAMPP and website development
articles.summary: Understand the web stack separately from the game database.
articles.scope: Apache Friends Windows FAQ; database connections for a specific Shaiya website require that website's own documentation.

blocks.heading: What XAMPP supplies
blocks.body: XAMPP supplies a local web-development stack and a control panel for its services. Apache Friends documents that its database distribution uses MariaDB rather than Microsoft SQL Server.

blocks.heading: How this relates to Shaiya
blocks.body: A website template using Microsoft SQL Server needs a compatible driver and connection setup; installing XAMPP does not supply the game's SQL Server databases. Review the template's PHP and database requirements before choosing a stack. This library does not connect a website to a game server automatically.

articles.title: When SQL will not connect
articles.summary: Separate the error category before changing settings.
articles.scope: Microsoft connectivity guidance plus inspected EP6.4 database configuration keys. No universal port or credential is prescribed.

blocks.heading: Collect the exact failure
blocks.body: Record which component failed, when it failed, and the error text with credentials removed. Check the SQL instance and service state, endpoint/name resolution, authentication, network rules and TLS requirements. Different causes require different fixes.

blocks.heading: Compare the application configuration
blocks.body: The inspected package has distinct UserData, GameData and GameDef connection settings. A successful login in SSMS does not establish that each game service uses the same endpoint, identity or database. Compare those settings deliberately.

blocks.heading: Change one variable at a time
blocks.body: Retest the same connection after each change. Keep the prior configuration available. Avoid replacing several binaries or changing unrelated ports while diagnosing a single database error.

articles.title: A useful development problem report
articles.summary: Give enough context to reproduce the issue.
articles.scope: Suggested reporting checklist; it does not diagnose or repair a running server.

blocks.heading: Include the baseline
blocks.body: State the episode and region, source archive, client/server build, operating system, SQL version and tool version. Describe the expected behavior, the observed behavior and the smallest steps that reproduce it.

blocks.heading: Include relevant evidence
blocks.body: Attach the exact error and a short sanitized log excerpt. Mention the last change and whether the issue also occurs with the untouched baseline. Do not include passwords, connection secrets or player records.

blocks.heading: Before trying a proposed fix
blocks.body: Keep a recoverable copy and test the proposed change in a separate environment. A suggestion for another episode or database layout is not automatically a fix for yours.

articles.title: Classes and faction names
articles.summary: The twelve class names in the current publisher overview.
articles.scope: Fawkes English overview, reviewed November 2026. Names and balance can differ in other localizations or private builds.

blocks.heading: Alliance of Light
blocks.body: The publisher lists Fighter, Defender, Priest, Archer, Mage and Ranger.

blocks.heading: Union of Fury
blocks.body: The corresponding Fury roster is Warrior, Guardian, Pagan, Assassin, Oracle and Hunter.

blocks.heading: For developers
blocks.body: Keep the client language and target build alongside any class-ID mapping. This roster does not establish database numeric IDs or a universal skill balance.

articles.title: Faction warfare, blessing and difficulty
articles.summary: Separate the published game concepts from build-specific rules.
articles.scope: Publisher overview only. Exact mode restrictions, resurrection exceptions, percentages and level caps need a version-specific source.

blocks.heading: Faction objectives
blocks.body: The publisher describes opposing-faction altar destruction as contributing to faction-wide Goddess Blessing buffs.

blocks.heading: Difficulty
blocks.body: Its overview describes several difficulty modes and permanent-death risk in Ultimate Mode. Check the rules and available resurrection items of the actual service before relying on that summary.

blocks.heading: Do not infer constants
blocks.body: The overview is not a specification for blessing formulas, stat points or private-server settings. No such numbers are asserted here.

articles.title: Windows services versus game health
articles.summary: A running service and a healthy game session are different checks.
articles.scope: Windows service concepts, applied as diagnostic guidance to Shaiya installations that register services.

blocks.heading: What Windows tracks
blocks.body: The Service Control Manager records installed services, starts them and maintains their reported state.

blocks.heading: Check the application too
blocks.body: For a Shaiya test installation, separately check the service state, its recent log and the expected login/game behavior. A Running label alone does not prove that SQL authentication or client compatibility succeeded.

blocks.heading: Capture before changing
blocks.body: Record the failing service name and exact log message. Compare one controlled restart with its timestamps instead of reinstalling every component.

articles.title: EP6.4: follow database configuration keys
articles.summary: Locate the database settings in the inspected server package.
articles.scope: Static EP6.4 Essentials inspection; configuration text establishes keys, not all runtime behavior or correct credentials.

blocks.heading: Keys observed
blocks.body: The inspected ps_login.ini has a UserData database key. ps_game.ini has GameDef and GameData; ps_dbAgent.ini has GameData. These are configuration entry names, not credentials to reuse.

blocks.heading: Trace a failure
blocks.body: When a log identifies a database connection failure, locate the corresponding service configuration and compare its intended database with your local deployment. Preserve a copy before editing.

blocks.heading: Duplicate templates
blocks.body: The package contains configuration in multiple directories. Establish which copy the running service reads before changing a value.

articles.title: MDF, NDF and LDF: what the files mean
articles.summary: Understand physical database files before moving a server.
articles.scope: SQL Server storage concepts; file names alone do not prove the schema or episode of a Shaiya database.

blocks.heading: Data and transaction log
blocks.body: A SQL Server database has data and transaction-log storage. MDF is the recommended extension for the primary data file, NDF for optional secondary files and LDF for the log.

blocks.heading: Logical versus physical names
blocks.body: The name SQL Server uses for a database file and its operating-system path are separate identifiers. Moving a downloaded package to another drive does not automatically update SQL Server file locations.

blocks.heading: Practical boundary
blocks.body: Treat the LDF as database recovery data, not a disposable text log. Use supported backup/restore procedures when preparing a test copy.

articles.title: Restore a separate test database
articles.summary: Create a safe target for inspecting legacy queries.
articles.scope: SQL Server backup/restore guidance. This is not an automated Shaiya migration recipe.

blocks.heading: Use another name and location
blocks.body: SQL Server can restore a backup into a separate database and different file paths. In SSMS, inspect both the target database name and every destination data/log path before starting.

blocks.heading: Avoid the live target
blocks.body: Use a dedicated test instance where possible. Do not select overwrite options merely to bypass a warning; inspect why the backup and target differ.

blocks.heading: After restoration
blocks.body: Review database access and application configuration before connecting a test service. A restored database is not proof that its client and server binaries match.

articles.title: Backup verification is not a restore test
articles.summary: Know what a successful backup check actually establishes.
articles.scope: SQL Server RESTORE VERIFYONLY documentation. No backup is executed by this reader.

blocks.heading: What it checks
blocks.body: RESTORE VERIFYONLY checks that a backup set is complete and readable without restoring the database.

blocks.heading: What it does not prove
blocks.body: Microsoft explicitly distinguishes this from checking the structure of all data in the backup. Success is not proof that the restored Shaiya application will behave correctly.

blocks.heading: Recommended validation
blocks.body: Keep a separate restoration test and an application smoke-test checklist. Record the backup date, SQL version and test outcome.

articles.title: Transactions, commit and rollback
articles.summary: Why reviewing the scope of an UPDATE matters.
articles.scope: SQL Server transaction semantics; a database transaction does not coordinate client archives or unrelated game-service memory.

blocks.heading: The unit of work
blocks.body: A successful transaction commits its database changes; a rolled-back transaction cancels its changes. SQL Server supports autocommit, explicit and implicit transaction modes.

blocks.heading: For query review
blocks.body: Before running a legacy modification, identify its target database and selection condition. Preview the intended rows on a test copy. Do not assume several pasted statements are one transaction.

blocks.heading: Limit of rollback
blocks.body: Do not present rollback as an undo button for changes already committed or edits to separate client files. Plan the complete test and recovery procedure before a live update.

articles.title: Database roles and access scope
articles.summary: Understand permissions without granting every account full control.
articles.scope: General SQL Server roles. Required Shaiya service permissions must be established for the actual package.

blocks.heading: Database-level roles
blocks.body: Database roles group permissions within a database. SQL Server provides fixed roles and lets administrators define custom roles.

blocks.heading: Separate account purposes
blocks.body: A read-only inspection account, a game-service login and an administrator can have different needs. Do not assume that granting a broad role is the correct response to every connection error.

blocks.heading: Check the target
blocks.body: Review the mapped user and its role membership in the intended database. A role change in one database does not establish the right access in another.

articles.title: Text encoding when reading Shaiya data
articles.summary: Recognize encoding as part of the file format.
articles.scope: Parsec documented defaults; not a claim that every Shaiya client uses ASCII.

blocks.heading: Explicit inputs
blocks.body: Parsec documents ASCII as its default encoding and allows an encoding parameter. An episode choice and a language encoding are different settings.

blocks.heading: Preserve the original
blocks.body: Use an unchanged sample containing non-ASCII text when checking a conversion. Compare the original text after reading and saving a separate copy; a file opening successfully is not enough to prove correct characters.

articles.title: Editing structured data through JSON
articles.summary: Use an exported document as the starting point.
articles.scope: Parsec JSON workflow. Format support and episode coverage remain limited to the library documentation.

blocks.heading: Preserve fields
blocks.body: The author recommends exporting an existing parsed file to JSON before editing and importing it again, so its expected fields remain present.

blocks.heading: Test a small change
blocks.body: Keep the original and change one field in a copy. Validate the JSON, import it, reopen the output and compare the intended value. Conversion does not automatically synchronize SQL or another server data file.

articles.title: Map data: SVMAP and WLD editing areas
articles.summary: Know which parts of the editor to inspect.
articles.scope: The shStudio author manual. Availability and compatibility depend on the editor and file version.

blocks.heading: Server map sections
blocks.body: The manual documents SVMAP areas for monsters, NPCs, portals, spawns and safe areas.

blocks.heading: World content
blocks.body: It also documents WLD editing for field maps and dungeons. A map change may involve more than one resource; do not replace a WLD file and assume server map behavior is synchronized.

blocks.heading: Validation workflow
blocks.body: Compare one change in a separate test client/server pair, including entry, movement and the edited entity. Keep exact filenames and the editor version with the result.

articles.title: Workspace, archive and patch are separate outputs
articles.summary: Choose the output you actually intend to distribute.
articles.scope: shStudio author manual, with workflow guidance; no universal updater configuration is implied.

blocks.heading: Workspace
blocks.body: The manual describes a workspace as the extracted directory hierarchy of a client archive. It can also work with the SAH/SAF archive pair and generate archives or patches.

blocks.heading: Practical check
blocks.body: Verify where the edited file was saved, then inspect the actual output package. Test it against a clean matching client before distribution. Do not edit the same workspace from two editor instances.

articles.title: Identify a package with SHA-256
articles.summary: Record a file fingerprint alongside its name and version.
articles.scope: PowerShell file hashing. Matching a hash identifies bytes; it is not a malware scan or compatibility test.

blocks.heading: Why names are insufficient
blocks.body: Two downloads may share an episode label while containing different bytes. Record the publisher URL, file size and SHA-256 when comparing packages.

blocks.heading: Read-only example
blocks.body: Replace the sample path with an actual local archive. Get-FileHash reads the file and reports its digest. Compare it with a value from a trusted publisher.

blocks.heading: Keep the scope clear
blocks.body: A matching digest verifies the expected file content. It does not prove that an executable is safe or that a client works with your server.

articles.title: Review configuration changes with Git
articles.summary: Compare before and after without changing either file.
articles.scope: Git text comparison guidance. Avoid publishing credentials contained in configuration files.

blocks.heading: Compare local copies
blocks.body: git diff --no-index compares two filesystem paths even outside a repository. It is useful for reviewing changes to a redacted configuration copy.

blocks.heading: Read-only example
blocks.body: The command displays differences. A difference can produce exit code 1; that is expected for this comparison mode.

blocks.heading: Keep a meaningful record
blocks.body: Record why each setting changed and the test result. Binary differences do not automatically explain the meaning of a game-data change.

articles.title: Track scripts and documentation in VS Code
articles.summary: Keep a reviewable history of your own project changes.
articles.scope: VS Code source-control documentation; recommended workflow for scripts and notes you are authorized to store.

blocks.heading: Review before committing
blocks.body: VS Code provides source-control views for reviewing changes, staging files and committing with Git.

blocks.heading: Organize the project
blocks.body: Keep your SQL source, documentation and redacted configuration templates in small, purposeful commits. Write the reason for the change rather than only its date.

blocks.heading: Exclude local data
blocks.body: Keep database dumps, private credentials and generated client archives out of ordinary source commits. Review the staged diff before pushing.

articles.title: Resolved in Parsec: item field serialization
articles.summary: A maintainer-documented fix for specific item layouts.
articles.scope: Parsec v1.1.1 release notes. The fix was documented by its maintainer; no affected client was run as part of this article review.

blocks.heading: Documented issue and fix
blocks.body: Version 1.1.1 adds EP6_4 and changes Item ReqLuc to uint for EP6_4 and above. It also corrects Item Range serialization to byte for EP5 and below.

blocks.heading: When relevant
blocks.body: If an older Parsec-based tool mishandles these fields, compare its dependency version with this release. This does not establish that unrelated tools or every corrupt Item.SData have the same cause.

blocks.heading: Verify locally
blocks.body: Test the updated dependency against an original affected sample and reopen a saved copy. Keep the old file until that comparison succeeds.

articles.title: Resolved in Parsec: archive paths and DbItemSell
articles.summary: Two concrete fixes recorded in version 1.2.0.
articles.scope: Parsec v1.2.0 release notes; maintainer confirmation, not a reproduction on the user's client.

blocks.heading: Documented fixes
blocks.body: The maintainer records a directory-separator correction when modifying SAH and a correction to DbItemSell structure reading/writing.

blocks.heading: Use the scope
blocks.body: Check whether your utility actually uses Parsec and which version it embeds. Updating an unrelated executable does not apply this library fix.

blocks.heading: Verification
blocks.body: On a copy, repeat the failing operation and inspect paths or affected records before promoting the output. Do not reinterpret all archive errors as this particular bug.

articles.title: Resolved in Parsec: text export and monster records
articles.summary: Fixes reported by the maintainer for version 1.1.0.
articles.scope: Parsec v1.1.0 release notes. These are library-specific fixes, not a general repair script.

blocks.heading: Published corrections
blocks.body: The release lists fixes for default CSV encoding, non-ASCII JSON escaping, MonsterRecord structure and reading all DBMonsterData fields.

blocks.heading: Check before replacing
blocks.body: Identify the exact library version used by your tool. Preserve a minimal input that demonstrates the problem and compare exported text and records after updating.

blocks.heading: What remains unverified
blocks.body: No claim is made that this resolves every localization problem or every episode-specific monster layout.

articles.title: SQL 18456: follow the actual login failure
articles.summary: A documented diagnostic route instead of a universal password fix.
articles.scope: Microsoft SQL Server guidance. Applies when the underlying database reports error 18456; Shaiya login-screen messages alone do not prove this cause.

blocks.heading: Meaning
blocks.body: Error 18456 indicates a rejected authentication attempt. The SQL error log supplies details that can distinguish a missing login, invalid credentials or an unsuitable authentication mode.

blocks.heading: Documented resolution
blocks.body: Confirm the intended SQL instance and account. Follow the resolution for the recorded reason: correct the credentials, establish the intended login/access, or change authentication mode only when the application actually requires it. Mode changes require a SQL service restart.

blocks.heading: Verify the result
blocks.body: Retry the same connection after the targeted correction and inspect the log. Do not distribute passwords or replace every service configuration as a shortcut.

articles.title: SQL 4064: unavailable default database
articles.summary: A default-database problem can look like a login failure.
articles.scope: Microsoft SQL Server guidance; not evidence of a broken Shaiya account table.

blocks.heading: Meaning
blocks.body: The login cannot open its default database. Causes include unavailable database state, an incorrect name or missing user access.

blocks.heading: Documented route
blocks.body: In SSMS connection options, specify an existing database the account can access. An administrator can then inspect the default database, its state and user mapping, and correct the specific issue.

blocks.heading: Completion check
blocks.body: Reconnect using the intended application database and confirm access. Changing a default database does not repair an offline or damaged database; those causes need their own documented recovery steps.

articles.title: How to read a solution status
articles.summary: Know what has actually been established before applying advice.
articles.scope: Editorial policy for this library. A published fix and a test on your own deployment are different evidence.

blocks.heading: Maintainer-confirmed fix
blocks.body: A tool author explicitly lists the correction in a linked release. The article names that version and limits the claim to that tool.

blocks.heading: Vendor-documented resolution
blocks.body: The software vendor documents cause-specific diagnostic and resolution steps. Match the actual error and conditions first.

blocks.heading: Community reports
blocks.body: A community solution needs a traceable report that the proposed change solved the issue, plus its package/version context. Unconfirmed suggestions are not labeled resolved. Even a confirmed report is not proof for every deployment.
